item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — 10,000-ton safe harbor.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons or less per year is not “commercial deep seabed mining,” regardless of profitability, ecological damage, or cumulative industry-wide extraction.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel-by-vessel threshold.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide one project among several vessels and keep each below 10,001 tons.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Unspecified annual measurement period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or rolling 12-month period, making compliance calculations contestable and potentially allowing extraction on either side of a reporting boundary.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — No tonnage methodology.** The bill does not say whether tonnage is measured when material is severed, brought aboard, landed, or processed, or whether water, sediment, waste rock, and unusable material count.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** Companies could argue that collecting, lifting, test-mining, storing material underwater, or transferring it to another vessel is not “recovery,” particularly if no minerals are landed or sold.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Ambiguous attribution to a vessel.** Seabed mining may involve collectors, riser systems, support ships, and transshipment vessels; the bill does not specify which vessel is deemed to have recovered the material.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary and measurement are unclear.** Mining at exactly 200 meters is outside the definition, and the bill does not say whether depth is measured from sea level, mean low water, the vessel, or another reference point.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Subsoil may not be covered.** The language refers to resources recovered “from the seabed” but does not expressly include the subsoil, creating an argument that buried deposits or drilling operations fall outside the prohibition.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Other mineral resources” lacks boundaries.** The phrase could sweep in conventional offshore oil, gas, sand, or aggregates—or be challenged as unclear when applied to materials unlike polymetallic nodules.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — The responsible “Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines “Secretary,” and Section 6 separately names the Secretary of State, leaving unclear whether Commerce, NOAA’s administrator, Interior, or another official makes the risk determination.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — No determination procedure or deadline.** There are no criteria, evidentiary requirements, public process, judicial-review rules, or timetable for deciding that another activity poses “comparable” risks; until a determination is made, the activity may remain outside the definition.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — “Comparable risks” is indeterminate.** The bill does not identify the relevant risks, ecosystems, probability, severity, or comparison baseline, making determinations inconsistent and vulnerable to challenge.

13. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, limited liability companies, trusts, associations, and other common business forms unless a court treats them as corporations.

14. **Section 2(2) — Geographic incorporation gaps.** A corporation must be organized under the laws of a “State,” which may exclude entities organized under District of Columbia, territorial, tribal, or federal law because “State” is not defined to include them.

15. **Section 2(2) — Foreign-subsidiary loophole.** A U.S. company could conduct mining through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary that is not itself a “U.S. person”; the bill has no ownership, control, alter-ego, or anti-evasion rule.

16. **Section 2(3) — Covered-vessel exclusions.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less need not register, even if they recover more than 10,000 metric tons, and larger support, processing, or transshipment vessels may escape registration if not “equipped for recovery.”

17. **Section 2(3) — Gross-tonnage standard is unspecified.** “Gross tons” measures vessel volume rather than weight, and different domestic and international measurement systems can yield different figures; the bill does not identify the applicable convention.

18. **Section 3(a) — “Person” is undefined.** The prohibition uses the broader word “person,” while the bill defines only “U.S. person,” leaving uncertainty about which companies, entities, officers, and unincorporated organizations are liable.

19. **Section 3(a) — “In the United States” is unclear.** The bill does not define whether this includes territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, U.S.-flagged vessels, territories, or merely conduct physically occurring on land within the United States.

20. **Section 3(a) — Foreign actors abroad remain outside the prohibition.** A non-U.S. company operating through foreign personnel and vessels outside the United States is not covered, even if the project is financed by U.S. investors or its minerals ultimately enter the U.S. market.

21. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** It is uncertain whether financing, insuring, directing, contracting for, facilitating, transporting, processing, purchasing, or selling mined material counts, allowing companies to participate without operating the mining equipment themselves.

22. **Section 3(a) — No anti-assistance or anti-evasion provisions.** The bill does not expressly prohibit attempts, conspiracy, aiding and abetting, causing a violation, sham contracting, or restructuring undertaken to avoid the prohibition.

23. **Section 3(b) — Any pre-enactment exploration license may qualify.** The provision does not identify the issuing authority, so companies could claim exemptions based on licenses from foreign governments, the International Seabed Authority, or potentially other bodies.

24. **Section 3(b) — Exploration licenses become mining exemptions.** The exemption covers “mining conducted under” an exploration license even though such a license ordinarily authorizes exploration rather than commercial production, potentially converting old exploration rights into a broad grandfather clause.

25. **Section 3(b) — No limits on grandfathered operations.** The exemption has no expiration date, production cap, geographic limit tied expressly to the licensed area, or requirement that operations actually existed before enactment.

26. **Section 3(b) — Transfers and amendments are unaddressed.** A pre-enactment license could potentially be sold, renewed, expanded, or materially amended after enactment while retaining the exemption.

27. **Section 3(b) — License validity is not required.** The text does not say the exploration license must remain valid, lawful, or in good standing, creating disputes over expired, suspended, or defective licenses.

28. **Section 3(c) — Broad environmental-assessment exemption.** Any activity conducted “for the purpose” of environmental assessment is exempt, with no permit, scientific protocol, tonnage limit, independent oversight, or requirement that environmental assessment be its sole or primary purpose.

29. **Section 3(c) — Dual-purpose and commercial activity may qualify.** An operator could characterize test mining or resource evaluation as environmental assessment while collecting commercially useful data or minerals; the bill neither prohibits sale of recovered material nor limits the exemption’s duration.

30. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, management, and physical operation may be divided among several entities, allowing each to dispute responsibility for registration.

31. **Section 4(a) — Registration mechanics are missing.** The bill provides no registration deadline, required information, updating obligation, implementing authority, or procedure for vessels that become covered after operations begin.

32. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so failure to register, file a report, or submit an accurate report is not expressly subject to the bill’s civil or criminal penalties.

33. **Section 4(b) — Reporting obligation can be evaded through nonregistration.** Reports are required from “[e]ach registered operator,” which could be read not to impose a reporting duty on an operator that unlawfully failed to register.

34. **Section 4(b) — Reports are vague and self-certified.** “Describing the recovery activities” supplies no required measurements, locations, supporting records, testing method, or independent verification, and the bill does not expressly penalize false certification.

35. **Section 4 — No inspection or monitoring authority.** NOAA receives registrations and reports but is not given express authority to inspect vessels, audit records, require tracking equipment, subpoena information, or verify reported tonnage.

36. **Section 4 — No disclosure or interagency provisions.** The bill does not require reports to be public or authorize routine sharing with enforcement agencies, limiting their usefulness for outside scrutiny and enforcement.

37. **Section 5(a) — No enforcement official or procedure is designated.** The bill creates civil liability but does not say which department may assess or sue for penalties, what process applies, or where an action may be brought.

38. **Section 5(a) — Daily penalties do not fit the annual threshold cleanly.** Because illegality depends on exceeding an annual tonnage threshold, it is unclear on which day a violation begins, whether earlier extraction becomes retroactively unlawful, and how many violation days should be counted.

39. **Section 5(a) — Maximum-only penalty may be inadequate.** The provision has no minimum penalty, disgorgement, remediation requirement, or adjustment for inflation, so a penalty could be far below the value of a mining project.

40. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” compounds the bill’s ambiguities.** Criminal prosecution may require proof that a defendant knew its conduct was unlawful, which will be difficult where terms such as “recovery,” “per year,” “engage in,” and the exemptions are unsettled.

41. **Section 5 — Limited remedies.** The bill does not expressly authorize injunctions, vessel detention or forfeiture, permit revocation, seizure of minerals, restoration orders, or recovery of enforcement and environmental-response costs.

42. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Conflicting timing language.** Section 5 refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but the entire Act does not take effect for 180 days; the mismatch invites disputes over whether conduct during that interval is prohibited or penalizable.

43. **Section 6 — Negotiation duty is largely unenforceable.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires only an effort, not an agreement or even commencement of formal negotiations, and the bill supplies no reporting requirement or consequence for inaction.

44. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” international prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether equivalence concerns tonnage, persons covered, exemptions, penalties, duration, or environmental effect.

45. **Section 7(a) — Termination standard is vague.** “Serious harm” is undefined, and the provision does not specify whether “without” means no risk at all, no expected harm, or harm mitigated to an acceptable level.

46. **Section 7(a) — National Academies report requirements are missing.** The bill does not require Congress or an agency to commission the report, set its scope or scientific standard, establish a deadline, or require that it actually recommend lifting the prohibition.

47. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution mechanism is underspecified.** The bill provides no expedited procedure, required text, committee deadlines, or explanation of what it means for Congress to act “on” the Academies’ report, creating procedural uncertainty.

48. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — The 10-year sunset overrides the stated safety condition.** Although subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a no-serious-harm finding, subsection (b) terminates the entire Act after 10 years even if Congress never makes that finding.

49. **Section 7(b) — No transition or savings clause.** The bill does not expressly preserve pending investigations, civil cases, penalties, reporting records, or liabilities after sunset, inviting litigation over whether unfinished enforcement may continue.

50. **Section 8 — Six-month pre-effective-date window.** Companies may expand extraction, obtain or transfer qualifying exploration licenses, or restructure operations during the 180 days before the Act takes effect; the bill contains no anti-stockpiling or anti-evasion rule for that period.
